lines.text: How much does one extra meter lift a rope around the Earth?
Wrap a rope around the Earth, flat on the ground, all the way around the equator.
That's forty thousand kilometers of rope.
Now add one meter. Just one. And pull it tight again, so it floats at the same height all the way around the planet.
How high does it rise? Almost everyone gives the same answer.
Nothing. One meter spread over forty million meters. You couldn't see it, not even with a magnifying glass.
It rises sixteen centimeters. Everywhere on the planet, at once.
You could stand your phone upright under that rope.
And the math fits on one line.
The length of a circle is two pi times the radius.
Make the rope one meter longer, and the radius grows by that meter divided by two pi.
Two pi is six point two eight.
One meter divided by six point two eight is sixteen centimeters.
Now look at what's missing from that math.
The size of the Earth. It isn't there.
It doesn't matter what you wrap.
Shrink the planet down to a tennis ball. Down to a marble.
The same extra meter still gives you the same sixteen centimeters.
We get it wrong because we think in percentages. And there's no percentage here.
The gap doesn't depend on what you wrap around, only on what you add.
One meter of rope is always sixteen centimeters of gap.
Around the Sun, around the Earth, or around your wrist.
And you can test it today.
Wrap a string around your wrist, add one meter, and pull it tight.
It will stand sixteen centimeters off your skin, exactly like it does around the planet.
So what did you guess, before you saw the number? Tell me in the comments.
